body:
Why electromagnetic waves matter in defence

Modern defence systems depend on the ability to obtain information, communicate over long distances and identify changes in the surrounding environment. Radar stations, wireless communication systems, navigation receivers and many surveillance instruments use electromagnetic energy to perform these functions.

Electromagnetic waves are disturbances involving changing electric and magnetic fields. They carry energy and can travel through a vacuum, including outer space.

This property distinguishes electromagnetic waves from sound waves. Sound is produced by vibrations and requires a material medium, such as air, water or a solid, for transmission. Electromagnetic waves do not require such a medium. This is why a satellite can communicate with a ground station across the vacuum of space.

Electricity and magnetism are closely related. A current-carrying conductor produces a magnetic field, while changing electric and magnetic fields are involved in electromagnetic-wave propagation. These principles provide the scientific foundation for radio communication and radar technology.

Frequency, wavelength and the electromagnetic spectrum

An electromagnetic wave has a frequency, meaning the number of complete oscillations occurring in 1 second. Frequency is measured in hertz (Hz). A wave also has a wavelength, the distance between corresponding points of successive waves.

In a vacuum, electromagnetic waves travel at approximately 300,000 km per second. At this constant speed, higher frequency means shorter wavelength, while lower frequency means longer wavelength.

The electromagnetic spectrum includes radio waves, microwaves, infrared radiation, visible light, ultraviolet radiation, X-rays and gamma rays. Microwaves are commonly treated as a part of the broader radio-frequency region, although they are also shown separately in spectrum classifications.

Radio waves and microwaves

Radio-frequency signals are especially important for wireless communication, radar and satellite links. A transmitter places information onto a radio-frequency carrier, and a suitable receiver extracts the information. Different systems use different authorised frequency bands because their communication needs and operating conditions vary.

Radar uses electromagnetic waves to detect objects. In a basic active-radar system, the equipment transmits a signal and examines the returning echo. The presence and characteristics of the echo can provide information about an object. Radar is therefore primarily a sensing system, although the information it produces may subsequently be transmitted through a communication network.

Visible light and infrared radiation

Visible-light sensors record information from the small part of the spectrum that the human eye can detect. They are useful for observing terrain, buildings, vehicles and other surface features when illumination and atmospheric conditions permit.

Infrared sensors detect infrared radiation, which is associated with thermal emission as well as reflected radiation in some infrared bands. Thermal infrared observations can help identify differences in temperature. Certain early-warning systems use infrared sensors to recognise the heat associated with missile launches.

Ultraviolet radiation, X-rays and gamma rays are also electromagnetic radiation, but they are not the principal bands used for ordinary long-range military radio communication.

Signals, noise and interference

A signal is an electromagnetic transmission or measurement that carries useful information. Noise is an unwanted disturbance that makes the information harder to detect or interpret. Interference occurs when unwanted energy affects the reception or interpretation of a signal.

Interference may arise unintentionally, such as when radio equipment is poorly coordinated, or deliberately, when someone attempts to interfere with another system. An interrupted radio link does not, by itself, prove that an enemy has attacked it.

Communication transfers information between users. Radar detects objects by examining electromagnetic returns. Electronic warfare concerns the use, observation, disruption and protection of electromagnetic-spectrum activity in military operations.

Prelims focus

  • Electromagnetic waves can propagate through a vacuum; sound waves require a material medium.
  • Frequency is measured in hertz (Hz).
  • At a fixed propagation speed, higher frequency corresponds to shorter wavelength.
  • Radar commonly uses radio-frequency or microwave signals to detect objects.
  • Infrared sensing can detect thermal differences and support early-warning applications.
  • Trap: Every radio interruption is not necessarily intentional jamming.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 12, Magnetic Effects of Electric Current, printed pp. 195–196; NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 12, Sound, printed pp. 160–161; NASA Science, Introduction to the Electromagnetic Spectrum and Anatomy of an Electromagnetic Wave, consulted 14 November 2026; International Telecommunication Union, Preventing Harmful Radio Interference, Overview and Radio Interference sections, consulted 14 November 2026.]

body:
Meaning and purpose of electronic warfare

Electronic warfare (EW) involves military activities that use, observe or control electromagnetic energy to understand an operational environment, reduce an adversary's effective use of the electromagnetic spectrum or preserve the effective use of that spectrum by friendly forces.

Electronic warfare is important because modern military organisations rely heavily on radar, wireless communication, navigation signals and electronic sensors. A force may possess advanced equipment but still experience serious difficulties if it cannot detect important signals, communicate reliably or trust the information received by its electronic systems.

Electronic warfare is commonly understood through 3 complementary functions: electronic support, electronic attack and electronic protection. These functions are related but have different immediate purposes.

Electronic support: observing electromagnetic activity

Electronic support (ES) involves searching for, detecting, identifying, locating or analysing electromagnetic emissions to obtain information. It is generally associated with passive reception rather than deliberately transmitting a signal to disturb another system.

For example, an electronic-support receiver may detect radio or radar emissions and help identify the general type of emitting system. The information may contribute to situational awareness or warning.

Two related intelligence terms are useful:

  • Communications intelligence (COMINT) concerns information obtained from communication-related signals.
  • Electronic intelligence (ELINT) commonly concerns information obtained from non-communication electromagnetic emissions, particularly radar-related signals.

Electronic support does not mean that every intercepted signal has been understood or decrypted. Detecting that a transmitter is operating and understanding the content of its message are different achievements.

Electronic attack: interfering with an adversary's electronic systems

Electronic attack (EA) involves actions intended to prevent, reduce or mislead an adversary's effective use of electromagnetic-spectrum-dependent systems.

Jamming

Jamming is deliberate electromagnetic interference intended to impair reception or operation. At the conceptual level, it can be understood as the introduction of unwanted electromagnetic energy that makes a useful signal more difficult to receive or interpret.

Jamming can affect radio communication, radar or navigation reception. Its effects depend on the circumstances and the systems involved; the existence of an interfering transmission does not guarantee that the affected system will stop functioning.

Electronic deception

Electronic deception attempts to mislead a receiving system rather than merely make reception difficult. The central distinction is between preventing reliable reception and causing incorrect interpretation.

For example, a receiver that cannot recover useful information is experiencing a different problem from a receiver that accepts misleading information as genuine. Both conditions may be associated with electronic attack, but they are not identical.

Electronic protection: maintaining friendly capability

Electronic protection (EP) consists of measures intended to preserve the effective operation of friendly electronic systems in the presence of interference, deception or other electromagnetic threats.

Protection may include suitable equipment design, monitoring of signal quality, appropriate use of authorised communication channels, reliable identification of expected signals and alternative means of maintaining essential communication. These are general protective principles; no single measure protects against every threat.

Older textbooks often use the terms electronic support measures (ESM), electronic countermeasures (ECM) and electronic counter-countermeasures (ECCM). For introductory study, ESM corresponds broadly to electronic support, ECM to electronic attack and ECCM to protective measures. These historical terms should not be confused with entirely separate domains.

Comparing the 3 functions

FunctionMain purposeTypical result
Electronic supportObserve and interpret emissionsInformation or warning
Electronic attackDisrupt or mislead opposing systemsReduced or unreliable reception
Electronic protectionMaintain friendly electronic operationImproved reliability or resistance

These functions can operate together. Electronic support may reveal an important emission; electronic attack concerns whether an opposing system can use electromagnetic energy effectively; electronic protection addresses whether friendly systems can continue operating. Identifying a threat, disrupting a threat and protecting against a threat are separate tasks.

Electronic warfare and ordinary radio interference

The electromagnetic spectrum is shared by many civilian, scientific and government services. The International Telecommunication Union (ITU) provides international radio regulations and coordination mechanisms intended to reduce harmful interference.

An accidental technical conflict between radio systems is not automatically electronic warfare. Intent, circumstances and the nature of the activity matter. Moreover, a legal allocation of spectrum does not by itself make a communication system resistant to deliberate hostile interference.

Prelims focus

  • Electronic support collects information from electromagnetic emissions.
  • Electronic attack includes jamming and electronic deception.
  • Electronic protection aims to preserve friendly use of electromagnetic systems.
  • COMINT relates to communication signals; ELINT commonly relates to non-communication electronic emissions.
  • ESM, ECM and ECCM are established older electronic-warfare terms.
  • Trap: Passive detection of a radar emission is electronic support, not automatically electronic attack.

[Sources: DRDO/DESIDOC, Electronic Warfare, 1988, Chapter 2, Electronic Warfare Definitions, sections 2.1.1–2.1.9; R. Pitchammal and S. Sarala, A Blue Print for the Future Electronic Warfare Suite Development, Defence Science Journal, Volume 63, Number 2, March 2013, pp. 192–193; International Telecommunication Union, Preventing Harmful Radio Interference, Radio Interference section, consulted 14 November 2026.]

title: Electronic Warfare: Support, Attack and Protection

body:
Why defence communication must be dependable

Defence communication connects personnel, ships, aircraft, ground stations and command centres. It allows information to reach the people who need it and enables coordinated responses. A useful communication system must deliver information to the intended recipient with sufficient accuracy and within an appropriate time.

Communication often forms part of a larger command-and-control system. Sensors obtain information, communication networks carry that information, personnel or authorised systems evaluate it, and decisions are conveyed to the relevant units.

The information can take several forms, including voice messages, text, position reports, sensor observations and images. The communication network does not necessarily produce this information; it may simply carry data generated elsewhere.

How different communication paths work

Terrestrial wireless communication

Radio equipment transmits information through electromagnetic waves between suitable antennas. Some radio systems, particularly many microwave links, depend strongly on a relatively unobstructed line of sight between antennas. Terrain, distance and atmospheric conditions can affect reception.

Radio systems operating in other bands may behave differently, including through reflection or other propagation effects. It is therefore inaccurate to claim that all radio communication requires a completely unobstructed visual path.

Satellite communication

A communication satellite can provide a link between locations separated by great distances or difficult terrain. A ground or mobile terminal transmits a signal towards the satellite through an uplink. The satellite processes or relays the information, and a downlink carries it to a receiving terminal.

For example, a ship at sea may use satellite communication to exchange information with a shore-based command centre. The satellite acts as a communication link; it does not have to photograph the ship to support this exchange.

Satellites in geostationary orbit are particularly useful when a communication service requires broad regional coverage and a nearly fixed direction for ground antennas. However, the greater distance to such satellites also contributes to transmission delay.

Optical-fibre communication

Optical fibre transmits information using light through a physical cable. It can carry large amounts of information over long distances and is useful for connecting fixed installations and communication networks.

Unlike a radio or satellite link, a fibre connection does not broadcast its information through open radio space along the cable. Nevertheless, the connected equipment and networks still need protection against unauthorised access and physical disruption.

What makes communication secure?

Secure communication aims to ensure that information reaches the appropriate recipient without unauthorised disclosure or undetected alteration. Security must also consider whether essential services remain available.

  • Encryption converts readable information into a protected form so that unauthorised parties cannot readily understand it without the necessary key.
  • Authentication helps establish whether a message or communicating party is genuine.
  • Integrity protection helps reveal whether information has been improperly changed.
  • Availability measures aim to keep the service usable, including when a link or component fails.

These protections address different problems. Encryption protects information from unauthorised reading, but it does not guarantee that a radio transmission will reach its destination. Authentication helps identify genuine messages, but it is not a substitute for an available communication channel.

Encryption and resistance to jamming are not the same. A radio message may remain confidential because it is encrypted while still becoming unavailable because its physical transmission is disrupted.

Resilience through alternative links

Defence networks often need to function under difficult conditions, including equipment faults, natural disasters and interference. A general way to improve reliability is to avoid dependence on a single component or communication path.

Where available, communication through terrestrial radio, satellite services and fixed networks can complement one another. If a particular route becomes unavailable, an authorised alternative may preserve essential communication. The precise alternative depends on the network and the circumstances.

Prelims focus

  • An uplink carries a signal towards a communication satellite; a downlink carries it towards a receiver.
  • A communication satellite relays information and is not necessarily an imaging satellite.
  • Optical fibre carries information as light through a physical medium.
  • Encryption supports confidentiality; authentication helps verify identity or origin.
  • Alternative communication paths can improve availability.
  • Trap: Encryption alone cannot prevent deliberate radio interference.

[Sources: NCERT, Fundamentals of Human Geography, Class 12, Chapter 8, Transport and Communication, printed pp. 78–79; NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12, Chapter 10, Transport and Communication, printed p. 123; ISRO, GSAT-7, Communication Payload and Mission sections, consulted 14 November 2026; National Institute of Standards and Technology, Information Security glossary and Special Publication 1800-26, Executive Summary, consulted 14 November 2026.]
